extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, examiners, and policymakers operating under Indonesian patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory notes and standards from the Indonesian Patent Law (Law No.13/2016) covering patentability requirements, procedural timelines, criminal provisions, investigatory powers, filing/formalities, exclusions, and application content requirements for patents in Indonesia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory injunction: notification of refusal
rubrics_metrics.description: When an interlocutory injunction is refused, a judge notifies the party requesting the interlocutory injunction with reasons for the refusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute requirement to provide reasons to requesting party; part of procedural fairness when injunction is denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory injunction: summons timeline and evidence submission
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Commercial Court issues an interlocutory injunction, it must summon affected parties within 7 days from issuance; affected parties may submit statements and evidence concerning the patent within 7 days from receipt of the subpoena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tight short deadlines (7 days) for summons and submissions following issuance of interlocutory injunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory injunction: judge's 30-day decision duty
rubrics_metrics.description: A judge must decide to reaffirm or cancel an interlocutory injunction not later than 30 days from the date of issuance of the interlocutory injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court must resolve the interlocutory injunction status within 30 days, ensuring prompt resolution of provisional measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory injunction: consequences if reaffirmed
rubrics_metrics.description: If an interlocutory injunction is reaffirmed, the cash deposit paid must be returned to the plaintiff; the plaintiff may request compensation for damages due to patent infringement and/or report the infringement to State Police or civil servant investigators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reaffirmation restores deposit and preserves plaintiff's rights to seek damages and initiate criminal reporting/enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interlocutory injunction: consequences if cancelled
rubrics_metrics.description: If an interlocutory injunction is cancelled, the cash deposit paid must immediately be forwarded to the party affected by the interlocutory injunction as compensation for damages caused by issuance of the interlocutory injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cancellation triggers immediate compensation to the affected (defendant) party via the deposit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigators' authority in patent criminal investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain civil servant investigators (in addition to State Police investigators) are vested with authority to investigate criminal offences in the field of patents and are authorized to: examine reports/statements; examine alleged persons; collect information/evidence; examine bookkeeping/records/documents; search/examine locations where evidence is located; confiscate materials/products resulting from infringement; request expert statements; request assistance from related institutions for arrest/seizure/wanted lists/prevent/repress; and terminate investigation where insufficient evidence is recovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List a–i in Article 159(2) enumerates explicit investigative powers. Confiscation and searches are expressly authorized when evidence is alleged to be located. Termination allowed where evidence insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigators: cooperation and reporting obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil servant investigators may request assistance from State Police investigators; they must inform the public prosecutor when initiating an investigation (copied to police) and must forward investigation results to the public prosecutor through the State Police investigators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights required coordination channels between civil servant investigators, police, and public prosecutors for criminal patent matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited actions against patented products and processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person without authorization from the patent holder is prohibited from producing, using, selling, importing, renting, handing over, or making available for sale/lease/transfer a patented product, and from using a patented production process to produce goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the scope of infringement acts (product and process) that are prohibited absent authorization of the patent holder (Article 160).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal penalties for patent infringement (standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who deliberately and without rights commit infringement (as per Article 160) for patents face imprisonment and/or fines: up to 4 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rp1,000,000,000 for patent; up to 2 years and/or fine up to Rp500,000,000 for simple patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties differ for full patent vs simple patent (Article 161–162). Sentences are stated as maximums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhanced penalties when infringement causes health/environment/death
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations that cause disruption in health and/or environment carry up to 7 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rp2,000,000,000; violations that cause human death carry up to 10 years imprisonment and/or fine up to Rp3,500,000,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal exposure is increased where infringement results in public harm or mortal consequences (Article 163(1)-(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalty for breaking confidentiality of application documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person who deliberately and without rights breaks confidentiality of an application document (Article 45(1)) is sentenced to imprisonment for a maximum of 2 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects confidentiality of patent application filings prior to publication/grant (Article 164).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal offences are 'warrant complaints'
rubrics_metrics.description: The criminal offences under Articles 161, 162, and 164 are warrants complaints (i.e., prosecuted on complaint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution requires a complaint; not necessarily ex officio prosecution (Article 165).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court may order confiscation and destruction of infringing goods
rubrics_metrics.description: If infringement is proven, a judge may order that goods resulting from patent infringement be confiscated by the State to be destroyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial remedial powers include destruction of infringing products (Article 166).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions for pharmaceutical importation/production near patent expiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions: (a) importation of patented pharmaceutical product legally marketed in another country is permitted if imported in accordance with legislation; (b) production of patented pharmaceutical product in Indonesia within five years before termination of patent protection for purpose of obtaining permits and marketing after patent termination is permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited carve-outs for pharmaceuticals to facilitate post-term market entry and regulatory processes (Article 167 a–b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual property consultant: definition and ministerial appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: An intellectual property consultant is a person with special skill in IP who provides filing and administration services; such consultants are appointed and dismissed by the Minister, with terms/procedures set by Ministerial Regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes regulated status and ministerial control over IP consultants (Article 168).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional rule: treatment of pending applications and existing patents
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Law comes into force, pending patent applications continue under previous legislation; simple patent applications filed under prior laws count term from grant date; patents granted under prior laws remain effective until their period ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures legal continuity and grandfathering for filings and granted patents under earlier statutes (Article 169).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementing regulations timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing regulation(s) of this Law must be stipulated not later than 2 years from promulgation; the Law comes into force upon promulgation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandates a two-year timeline for regulations needed to implement the Law (Article 171).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple Patent: eligibility and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple Patent is granted for an invention in the form of a product that is distinctive in technical features and retains more practical functions than previous invention due to its shape/configuration/construction/components, and may also be granted for a new process or method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines simple patent as suitable for simpler/less technically complex innovations with practical advantages (Article 3, elucidation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject matter: games and purely business methods
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Games’ means rules or methods related to human physical acts or activities; ‘business’ means business methods that do not have technical character or technical effect — these are unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excludes non-technical business methods and game rules absent a technical effect (Article 4 points 2–3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer program patentability requires technical character/effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer programs that only contain program code without technical character, technical effect, or problem-solving are excluded; if a computer program has instructions producing technical effects/functions to solve problems (tangible or intangible), it may be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that technical contribution/technical effect is necessary for software-related inventions (Article 4 point d). Examples given: algorithm definition and encrypting information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of prior art and 'existing or known product'
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Existing and/or known product’ comprises tools, goods, machines, compositions, formulas, methods, usage, substances, and systems whether patent-protected or in the public domain; 'state of the art' includes patent and non-patent literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art includes both patent and non-patent materials globally; used to assess novelty and inventive step (Article 4 f; Article 5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'not similar' for novelty assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'not similar' for novelty does not only mean different in form, but must be viewed in light of the function of technical features of the invention compared to prior inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty judged by functional/technical feature comparison rather than superficial differences (Article 5 section (1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority right: conditions for effectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Priority right of an application comes into effect provided all administrative and substantive requirements are fulfilled; for substantive requirements, the claimed element in the application must be disclosed in the priority document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority claims require that the priority document actually disclose the claimed elements; applies to first applications filed in member states/under PCT (Article 5 section (2), Article 7 section (2), Article 30).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive examination criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive examination (excluding simple patent provisions) determines compliance with novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability, unity of invention, clear disclosure, and that the subject is not an unpatentable invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerates the core substantive patentability requirements considered during examination (Article 5 section (3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Official and officially recognized exhibitions for novelty grace
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Official exhibition’ means exhibitions organized by the government; ‘officially recognized exhibition’ means public exhibitions recognized/approved by government — relevant to grace period rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibitions recognized by authorities can affect novelty/grace considerations (Article 6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-obviousness (inventive step) standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-obviousness is judged from the viewpoint of a person skilled in the art; an example is a toothbrush with a detachable head that can be replaced with a razor head — such an invention may be non-obvious to a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of realistic skilled-person examples to illustrate inventive step (Article 7 section (1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A product must be able to be produced continuously (mass production) with equal quality; a process must be able to be performed or used in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets practical producibility/useability as the benchmark for industrial applicability (Article 8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical methods exclusion and equipment exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods of examination (diagnosis) and methods of treatment in medical circumstances are excluded from patentability; however, health equipment (tools, materials, drugs) are excluded from this exclusion and can be patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between non-patentable therapeutic/diagnostic methods and patentable medical devices/drugs (Article 9 point b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Living organisms and biological vs microbiological processes definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Living organisms include human, animal, or plant; microorganisms are tiny organisms (amoeba, fungi, viruses, bacteria). ‘Biological processes essential to produce plant or animal’ refers to conventional/natural propagation (cuttings, layering, pollination) and are excluded; ‘non-biological or microbiological processes’ (transgenic/genetic engineering including chemical/physical/microorganism techniques) are treated differently (not excluded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies scope of biotechnology exclusions and what constitutes a patentable process versus excluded natural propagation (Article 9 points d–e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship, moral rights, and assignment rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventor naming is recognized as moral rights; 'person who gets the inventor's assigns' includes heirs via inheritance; 'inventor in an official relation' refers to civil state apparatus (ASN) and government institution definitions apply to ownership/assignment rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies moral rights and assignment/ownership nuances, especially for government-employed inventors (Articles 10–13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior user rights protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Protection is provided to previous users who in good faith used the invention but did not apply for a patent; the invention must be genuinely the result of activity carried out in good faith by the first user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior user is not an exclusive right holder but has lawful use protections (Article 14 and Article 16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of exclusive rights and imported products using patented processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive rights grant the patent holder the right to implement commercially or authorize others and to exclude others; if a product is imported to Indonesia and a process used to make it is patented, the patent-process holder is entitled to seek legal remedies against imported products, provided the product was produced in Indonesia using the patented process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains product v. process protection interplay for imported goods (Article 19 sections 1–2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and educational use exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Use for educational, research, experimental, or analytical purposes (including bioequivalence tests) is permitted provided it does not prejudice the proper interests of the patent holder (i.e., does not lead to commercial exploitation that would damage or create competitors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines a narrow experimental/educational exception and what 'does not prejudice' means (Article 19 section 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual fee (maintenance) and recording media definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Annual fee’ refers to the periodic fee payable by a patent holder each year (maintenance fee). ‘Recorded’ means recorded in the patent database. ‘Electronic media’ refers to media accessed electronically (websites); ‘non-electronic media’ refers to Patent Gazette or physical announcements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines maintenance obligations and how records/publication may be made (Articles 21–22).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple patent term rationale and duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple patents protect relatively simple/low-cost technological products/processes for 10 years, a period regarded sufficient for reasonable economic benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains policy rationale for shorter simple patent term compared to regular patents (Article 23).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention and linked inventions; electronic filing (IPAS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple new inventions that are strongly related (unity) may be filed in one application (e.g., new pen and new ink). Electronic applications are filed using the IPAS (Industrial Property Automation System).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides examples of unity and clarifies the electronic filing mechanism (Article 24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application components and requirement that claims be supported by description
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must describe the subject matter of the invention sought for protection and must be clearly elaborated and supported by the description. The application also requires abstract, drawings (technical drawing), and other standard components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes the support requirement between claims and description; defines 'abstract' and 'drawing' (Article 25 points c–e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genetic resources and traditional knowledge disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The origin of genetic resources and/or traditional knowledge related to the invention must be mentioned clearly and truthfully in the description to ensure resources/knowledge are not claimed by other countries and to encourage Access Benefit Sharing (ABS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandatory disclosure aimed at ABS and preventing misappropriation of genetic resources/traditional knowledge (Article 26).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing date importance and description definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing date is critical under first-to-file rules and is important for application status; 'description' means a written explanation on how to implement the invention so a person skilled in the field can understand it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing date certainty and sufficient description are central to priority and enablement (Article 34).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on extending scope of invention via amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'extend the scope of invention' means adding essence/subject, new information or removing technical features in description/drawings/claims that causes extension of claim scope — this is not permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments are restricted to prevent introducing new matter or broadening the claimed subject (Article 39 section 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention: handling of multiple inventions in one application
rubrics_metrics.description: An application containing multiple inventions that are not linked (lack unity) may result in rejection of the non-linked inventions; example provided where one application contains three inventions A, B, C and B and C are rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner may require division or reject non-unity claims; the provided example clarifies how multiple inventions are treated (Article 41).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient evidence standard for inventor attribution disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Sufficient evidence’ means convincing evidence to the Minister that the person is an inventor (e.g., affidavit of agreement between applicant and person claimed to be inventor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to adjudicate inventor entitlement disputes and protect inventors (Article 45 section 4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing, classification, and use of IPC
rubrics_metrics.description: Announcements/publication may be electronic or non-electronic; publication is carried out continuously during the period; classification of invention is intended to categorize applications by technology to aid search — Indonesia uses IPC in practice even if not ratified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification facilitates substantive examination and prior art searching (Article 47–48).

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion vs opposition definitions and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Opinion’ is unsolicited information from any person (written evidence, verbal elaboration, simulation) taken place in/abroad; ‘opposition’ is information conveyed following a request not to grant a patent on a relevant announced invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes unsolicited public input (opinion) from formal oppositions responding to announcements (Article 49).

rubrics_metrics.name: Security and defense related exclusion specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions related to security and defense (main equipment of defense system, firearms, ammunition, military explosives, interception, wiretapping, surveillance, encryption) are treated specially and may concern state interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines types of inventions that implicate national security considerations (Article 50).

rubrics_metrics.name: Required documents for patentability assessment and additional explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents such as comparative documents, search reports, and correspondence regarding examination results in origin country are required to facilitate assessment of novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability; 'additional explanation' may include applicant amendments based on search or preliminary examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets evidentiary and documentary support expectations for substantive examination (Article 55 sections 1–2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision timeframe for examination communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions are issued not later than 30 months since examination needs to be communicated several times with the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies a maximum timeframe (30 months) related to communication/examination decisions (Article 57).
